Sentence
sĕn´tens
n. (a judicial decision; rendering Greek krima and apokrima)
From Latin sententia, an opinion or judgment pronounced. In Scripture the word belongs to the bench, not the grammar book.

Biblical Definition

A sentence is a judgment pronounced. Ecclesiastes diagnoses the danger of a slow one: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecc 8:11). Paul describes his brush with death as having “the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead” (2Co 1:9). And at the Jerusalem council James renders one: “my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God” (Act 15:19) — a judgment that kept the gospel free.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sentence as a judgment pronounced by a court or judge upon a criminal; a determination or decision given.

expand to see more

SENTENCE, n. In law, a judgment pronounced by a court or judge upon a person on trial for a crime or offense.

2. A determination or decision given, particularly on some disputed point.

3. A short saying containing moral instruction; a maxim.

Key Scripture

Ecc 8:11 — "Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil."

2Co 1:9 — "But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead:"

Act 15:19 — "Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God:"

Deu 17:9 — "And thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and enquire; and they shall shew thee the sentence of judgment:"

Modern Corruption

Delayed judgment is read as no judgment — exactly the error Ecclesiastes names — while a culture of endless appeal teaches that no sentence is ever final.

expand to see more

Ecclesiastes 8:11 is one of the most useful verses in Scripture for reading a civilization. The mechanism is not that men conclude God does not exist; it is that the gap between the deed and the sentence is long enough for the conscience to lose the connection, and so hearts become fully set to do evil. God's patience, designed for repentance, is misread as approval — which is why 2 Peter has to insist that the Lord is not slack concerning his promise.

Paul's use inverts the terror. He received the sentence of death in himself, and names its purpose: that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead. For the believer, the sentence has already fallen on a Substitute, so the experience of dying becomes an instrument of faith rather than a foretaste of wrath. Same word, opposite outcome, and the cross is the difference.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek krima (G2917), a judicial decision; apokrima (G610), a sentence passed; Hebrew pithgam (H6599), a decree, in Ecclesiastes 8:11.

expand to see more

Greek apokrima (G610) — a judicial sentence; only 2 Corinthians 1:9.

Greek krima (G2917) — judgment, condemnation; Romans 5:16, the judgment was by one to condemnation.

Hebrew pithgam (H6599) — decree, sentence; Ecclesiastes 8:11, Esther 1:20.

Usage

"“Sentence… is not executed speedily” — delay misread as acquittal."

"“We had the sentence of death in ourselves” — a verdict that teaches faith."

"“My sentence is, that we trouble not them” — the ruling that kept the gospel free."
